Gesture Terrain:
## Gesture Terrain

### Project Header

# Gesture Terrain

**Movement accumulates as geological memory.**

A browser-based interactive artwork in which four hand gestures deposit, erode, fracture, and redirect a virtual landscape. Unlike an interface that resets after every command, the terrain retains each intervention and becomes a record of movement over time.

Independent project · 5 weeks · 2026  
Three.js · WebGL · GLSL · MediaPipe Hand Landmarker · JavaScript

Primary action: **Launch live work**  
Support text: Camera permission required · Desktop recommended · Video frames remain on device  
Fallback action: **Watch the interaction film**

### 01 — The Work

What if a gesture behaved like a geological force?

Gesture Terrain replaces short-lived visual feedback with an accumulating world. An open palm raises sediment, a fist erodes a basin, a pinch forms a fault or mineral vein, and a V sign draws a directional flow. Every accepted gesture is stored as a spatial event. As those events settle, they are baked into the terrain rather than removed.

The result is not a neutral control surface. It is a landscape with a history: touch becomes trace, and trace becomes terrain.

### 02 — Four Gestures, Four Forces

**Open Palm — Sediment / Growth**  
Deposits material and gradually raises the surface.

**Fist — Erosion / Basin**  
Pushes the surface downward to form an erosion basin.

**Pinch — Fault / Mineral**  
Creates a fissure and a concentrated mineral trace.

**V Sign — Directed Flow**  
Uses hand orientation to draw a directional channel across the surface.

### 03 — A Landscape That Remembers

Each recognised gesture creates a record containing position, radius, strength, direction, and settling time. Active records deform the mesh gradually. Settled records are incorporated into persistent height and geology buffers, so a new gesture never flattens earlier actions.

Two visual modes read the same memory differently. Concept mode exposes the landscape as a luminous computational field. Realism mode translates it into water, soil, grass, rock, mineral, sky, and cloud. Switching modes changes the interpretation, not the underlying terrain history.

### 04 — Technical Notes

The browser estimates 21 hand landmarks locally with MediaPipe. A transparent geometric classifier derives finger extension, pinch ratio, hand compactness, reach, movement velocity, position, and orientation. A 160 ms stability hold prevents brief predictions from modifying the terrain, while a 320 ms grace period absorbs short tracking losses.

In a preliminary single-participant study, 12 trials produced 658 labelled frames across four gestures and three camera distances under normal lighting. The geometric classifier labelled 632 frames correctly, reaching 96.0% frame-level accuracy and a macro F1 score of 0.974. Pinch was the weakest gesture at 85.3%.

Disclosure: this is exploratory evidence from one participant. It does not establish generalisation across people, lighting conditions, cameras, or environments.

### 05 — Reflection

The project began with the assumption that a learned gesture classifier would produce the most convincing interaction. Testing challenged that assumption. On the available evidence, transparent geometric rules were more accurate, easier to tune, and easier for a participant to understand.

Recognition accuracy became part of the artistic material rather than a separate engineering score. A gesture only feels like a force when the system responds consistently enough for cause and effect to remain legible.
Shape of Sound:
## Shape of Sound

### Project Header

# Shape of Sound

**One signal, five visual readings.**

A browser-based audio-reactive artwork that translates a locally loaded sound into five generative visual systems. Each system receives the same analysed signal but constructs a different image from it.

Independent project · 3 weeks · 2026  
p5.js · Web Audio API · JavaScript · HTML5 Canvas

Primary action: **Launch live work**  
Support text: Load audio from your device · Audio is processed locally  
Fallback action: **Watch the visual comparison**

### 01 — The Work

How many images can one sound contain?

Shape of Sound treats audio analysis as interpretation rather than transcription. A participant loads an audio file and moves between five visual systems. Amplitude, frequency balance, spectral brightness, and beat events remain consistent; what changes is the visual grammar used to read them.

The work makes those differences comparable. One signal can become an expanding surface, a radial body, an atmospheric flow, a field of painterly events, or a corridor that appears to advance and collapse.

### 02 — Five Visual Grammars

**Particle Ripple**  
Amplitude and bass move through an elliptical particle field as travelling waves.

**Spectral Bloom**  
Frequency bins become radial lengths; beat events create transient shards.

**Nebula Flow**  
Energy, frequency bands, and spectral brightness alter flow, turbulence, colour, and detail.

**Paint Splash**  
Beat strength becomes a sequence of discrete painterly bursts and persistent traces.

**Corridor**  
Spectrum snapshots form receding ridges while bass, treble, and spectral brightness alter depth, atmosphere, and the central vanishing point.

### 03 — Shared Signal Architecture

The Web Audio API provides time-domain and frequency-domain samples for every animation frame. The work derives RMS amplitude, bass, mid, and treble energy, spectral centroid, and adaptive beat events. Feature-specific smoothing keeps rhythmic events immediate while colour and atmosphere change more gradually.

The participant can adjust reactivity, trail length, beat sensitivity, saturation, brightness, and speed. These controls alter how strongly each visual system interprets the same signal; they do not change the audio itself.

### 04 — Comparison as Interaction

The five modes are separate modules around one shared player and analysis layer. This makes switching meaningful: the viewer does not select five unrelated effects, but compares five ways of turning measurement into visual form.

The public demonstration uses a clearly licensed audio source. The live work also accepts local MP3, WAV, or OGG files; those files remain in the participant's browser and are not uploaded.

### 05 — Reflection

The project revealed that mapping is an authored decision. Frequency data does not naturally contain a flower, a nebula, a splash, or a corridor. Each image appears because the same measurements are given different spatial, temporal, and emotional rules.

The next development would narrow the number of visual systems and explore longer-form transitions between them, allowing one reading to transform into another without leaving the shared signal.

Fuzzy Boundaries:
## Fuzzy Boundaries

### Project Header

# Fuzzy Boundaries

**What remains visible when a classifier is not forced to decide?**

An interactive image artwork that turns Kernel Fuzzy C-Means membership values into a visual language, preserving the ambiguity normally discarded by an argmax decision.

Independent project · 3 weeks · 2026  
JavaScript · HTML5 Canvas · Kernel Fuzzy C-Means · RBF kernel

Primary action: **Launch live work**  
Support text: Use a preset, upload an image, or capture a camera frame  
Fallback action: **Watch the mode comparison**

### 01 — The Work

Classification systems often calculate a rich distribution and then show only the winning label. Fuzzy Boundaries keeps the distribution.

Every pixel is allowed to belong to several colour clusters at once. Soft Blend renders those simultaneous memberships as continuous mixtures. Hard Partition applies argmax and forces every pixel into one cluster. Entropy makes uncertainty itself visible: confident regions recede while contested borders glow.

### 02 — Three Ways of Seeing

**Soft Blend**  
Each pixel is coloured by the weighted combination of all cluster centres.

**Hard Partition**  
Each pixel is assigned to the cluster with its strongest membership.

**Entropy**  
Brightness follows normalised fuzzy entropy, bringing ambiguous areas forward.

Viewing the modes side by side makes the final classification decision perceptible. What appears as a clean boundary in Hard Partition is revealed as a field of partial belonging in Soft Blend and Entropy.

### 03 — The Viewer Controls the Boundary

A participant can choose a preset image, upload a local image, or capture one camera frame. Cluster count determines how many categories the image is asked to become. The fuzziness value m controls how strongly memberships overlap. Kernel width sigma controls the reach of similarity in RBF kernel space.

Hovering over the image reveals the full membership vector and fuzzy entropy at that point. The selected interpretation can be exported as a PNG.

### 04 — From Analytical Tool to Visual Material

The work grew from an undergraduate customer-clustering system. That system used Kernel Fuzzy C-Means to preserve degrees of customer membership during analysis, then converted them into operational segments through argmax.

Fuzzy Boundaries removes that final compression and changes the algorithm's material from customer vectors to image pixels. The mathematics remains related, but the purpose changes: the algorithm is used to inspect what classification hides rather than to deliver a final segment.

### 05 — Technical Notes

The browser samples 2,600 RGB pixels, initialises centres with K-Means++, and iterates RBF-kernel distances, fuzzy memberships, and kernel-weighted centres until convergence or 60 iterations. After fitting, membership and entropy are evaluated for every pixel in the working image.

The implementation supports 2–8 clusters, fuzziness values from 1.05 to 4, and kernel widths from 0.06 to 0.8. Fitting uses a reproducible pixel sample to keep the interaction responsive; the final render recomputes values across the full working image.

### 06 — Reflection

The project began with a technical observation: the membership matrix contained information that the clustering system calculated and then discarded. Moving that observation into an interactive image made the loss visible without asking a viewer to read a table of probabilities.

The work does not claim that colour clusters are equivalent to human identities. It uses the image as a bounded perceptual experiment in how continuous distributions become categorical output.
Systems & Research:
## Systems & Research

# Systems & Research

Selected engineering projects that support my computational arts practice through data analysis, full-stack development, and explainable AI workflows.

## KFCM Customer Clustering System

An undergraduate graduation project that turns e-commerce transactions into interpretable customer segments through a hand-built Kernel Fuzzy C-Means pipeline and a local analytical interface.

I implemented preprocessing, RFM plus return-rate features, KFCM with an RBF kernel, comparison methods, membership exports, visual analysis, and automated reporting. The system processed 525,461 transaction records into 4,312 valid customer profiles. Its unresolved question—what is lost when fuzzy membership becomes one operational label—later became the starting point for Fuzzy Boundaries.

Suggested evidence: interface overview · computation flow · membership view · comparison metrics · relationship to Fuzzy Boundaries

## SkillDistill Studio

A full-stack AI workbench that turns long-form sources into inspectable, testable, and exportable Agent Skills. The workflow keeps source evidence, human review, revision history, evaluation cases, failure reasons, and export decisions visible.

In a recorded run using public-domain material, SkillDistill Studio turned 117 candidate records into 19 Skill specifications. Ten Skills entered a 21-case evaluation: seven passed and were exported, while three failed and were excluded. The run demonstrates how review and evaluation shape a release decision.

Suggested evidence: workflow overview · source anchors · review gates · visible failures · release decision

## About

# About

I am Huang Zijia, a creative technologist with a background in computer science. My practice uses interactive systems, generative media, data analysis, and AI to make computational processes perceptible.

I am especially interested in the moment when continuous input becomes a discrete decision: a hand becomes a recognised gesture, a sound becomes a set of measured features, or a membership distribution becomes one label. My recent works turn those translations into browser-based experiences that viewers can enter, adjust, and compare.

I completed a B.Eng. in Computer Science and Technology at Yangzhou University in 2026. Alongside my independent creative work, I have developed machine-learning interfaces, data visualisation systems, local-LLM integrations, and full-stack analytical tools. I hope to extend this practice towards interactive virtual worlds, games, and immersive media.
